title: The Widow's Gift and the Temple's End
summary: Jesus watches a poor widow put two small copper coins into the treasury and says she has given more than all the rich. When some admire the temple's beauty, he predicts that not one stone will be left on another, and then describes deceivers, wars, and persecution; Jerusalem surrounded by armies and trodden down by the Gentiles until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled; and signs in the heavens and the coming of the Son of Man. He tells them to endure, to watch, and to pray, and each day he teaches in the temple and each night lodges on the Mount of Olives.
story:
This is Jesus' last public teaching in Luke before the Passover and his arrest. It follows directly from his warning about scribes who defraud widows of their houses (20:47), and the widow who gives all she has to live on stands both as an example of devotion and as a witness against a system that should have cared for her. From the treasury the conversation moves to the temple itself, and Jesus looks ahead to two events that Luke keeps distinct: the siege and fall of Jerusalem, which came within a generation, and the coming of the Son of Man, which is set after ‘the times of the Gentiles’. Between them lies the long period of witness, persecution, and endurance that Luke will narrate in Acts, where the apostles are arrested, brought before synagogues, kings, and governors, and given words their opponents cannot resist.

Luke's version of the discourse differs from Mark 13 in setting and in shape. There is no move to the Mount of Olives and no private audience of four disciples; Jesus speaks in the temple, and verses 37 and 38 say he taught there every day and spent each night on the Mount of Olives while all the people came early to hear him. Those verses close the frame that began at 19:47-48, and chapter 22 opens with the leaders finding, through Judas, the way to arrest him apart from the crowd. The watchfulness Jesus commands here is tested within days, when he prays on the Mount of Olives and finds his disciples asleep (22:39-46).
historical:
The temple the disciples admired was Herod the Great's rebuilding of the second temple, begun about 20 or 19 BC (Josephus, Antiquities 15.380) and still being finished in the early 60s AD. Josephus describes its white stone and gold (Jewish War 5.184-227; Antiquities 15.380-425), and among the ‘consecrated gifts’ (anathēmata, verse 5, a word found only here in the New Testament) was a golden vine over the sanctuary entrance with clusters as tall as a man (Jewish War 5.210; Antiquities 15.395). The Babylonian Talmud preserves the saying that whoever has not seen Herod's building has never seen a beautiful building (b. Bava Batra 4a). The treasury was in the inner courts: the Mishnah describes thirteen trumpet-shaped chests for offerings (m. Shekalim 6:5), and Josephus places treasury chambers along the Court of the Women, open to all Israelites (Jewish War 5.200; compare John 8:20).

The decades after Jesus saw what the discourse describes. Josephus tells of popular prophets who promised signs of deliverance, among them Theudas around AD 45 (Antiquities 20.97-98) and the Egyptian who led a crowd to the Mount of Olives in the 50s (Antiquities 20.169-172; Acts 21:38). Famine struck Judea under Claudius (Acts 11:28; Antiquities 20.101), an earthquake devastated Laodicea in AD 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27), and Nero turned on the Christians of Rome in AD 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44). Josephus and Tacitus list portents said to have come before the city fell, including a star like a sword and armies seen in the clouds (Jewish War 6.288-300; Tacitus, Histories 5.13), which recall the ‘fearful sights and great signs from heaven’ of verse 11.

The revolt began in AD 66. That autumn the legate of Syria, Cestius Gallus, marched on Jerusalem, encamped against it, and attacked the temple's walls, then withdrew and was badly defeated in the pass of Beth-horon (Jewish War 2.499-555). The church historian Eusebius records that the Christians of Jerusalem, warned by an oracle, left before the war for Pella east of the Jordan (Ecclesiastical History 3.5.3), and many interpreters have connected the brief siege of 66, when the city was surrounded and then open, with the warning of verses 20 and 21, though Eusebius does not say so. Vespasian subdued Galilee and much of Judea in 67 and 68; Titus besieged Jerusalem in the spring of 70, enclosed it with a siege wall (Jewish War 5.499-511), and took it in the late summer. Josephus describes the famine inside the walls, including a woman who ate her own child (Jewish War 6.201-213), the burning of the temple, and the razing of the city. He puts the captives at 97,000, of whom the older were sent to labor in Egypt and many were sent to the provinces to die in the arenas (Jewish War 6.418-420), which answers to ‘led captive into all the nations’ (verse 24).

Jerusalem remained under Gentile rule for centuries. After the Bar Kokhba revolt (AD 132 to 135) Hadrian refounded it as the Roman colony Aelia Capitolina, and Eusebius says Jews were forbidden even to see the city from a distance (Ecclesiastical History 4.6.3). It passed to Byzantine, Arab, Crusader, Ayyubid, Mamluk, Ottoman, and British rule, was divided in 1948, and came under Israeli control in June 1967, which is why some modern readers have tied verse 24 to twentieth-century events.
cultural:
The widow's two coins were lepta, the smallest bronze coins in use in Judea; many in circulation were Hasmonean issues of Alexander Jannaeus from the first century BC. Mark explains that two made a Roman quadrans, a sixty-fourth of a denarius (Mark 12:42); Luke, writing for readers across the empire, leaves the explanation out. The English phrase ‘the widow's mite’ comes from the King James Version's ‘two mites’. Widows without sons or brothers had few means of support, and the early church soon organized daily provision for them (Acts 6:1, 1 Timothy 5:3-16). Jesus contrasts the rich, who gave out of their surplus (perisseuma), with the widow, who gave out of her lack (husterēma) all she had to live on (bios, her means of life).

The discourse speaks in the idiom of the prophets. Wars, earthquakes, famines, and plagues were the standard signs of judgment in Jeremiah and Ezekiel (Jeremiah 14:12, Ezekiel 14:21), and in Greek the pairing in verse 11 is a play on sound, limoi kai loimoi, ‘famines and pestilences’. Signs in the sun, moon, and stars and the shaking of the heavens were the prophets' language for God's decisive acts in history, used of the fall of Babylon (Isaiah 13:10) and Edom (Isaiah 34:4). The roaring sea was an ancient picture of chaos and of the nations in turmoil (Psalm 65:7, Isaiah 17:12), which only God can still. First readers would neither take such language as a weather report nor dismiss it as ornament; it announced that God was acting in a way that shook the world.

The practical warnings fit a Judean siege. A walled city was normally the refuge in war, and country people fled into it; Jesus reverses the instinct and tells those in the city to get out and those in the country to stay out (verse 21). Pregnant women and nursing mothers suffered most in flight and famine, as Lamentations 4:10 remembers of the Babylonian siege, and Jesus will say the same to the women of Jerusalem on the road to the cross (23:28-29). ‘Days of vengeance’ is the language of Hosea 9:7 and Deuteronomy 32:35 in the Greek Old Testament, where God's covenant judgment falls on his own people. To be ‘trodden down’ echoes the Greek of Zechariah 12:3, where Jerusalem is a stone trampled by the nations, and Daniel 8:13, where the sanctuary is trampled; 1 Maccabees 3:45 uses the same image of the sanctuary under Antiochus IV. The ‘times of the nations’ recalls Tobit 14:5, which foresees Israel's return and a second temple lesser than the first until the times of the age are fulfilled.

The fig tree, unlike most trees in the land, drops its leaves in winter, and its new leaves in late spring meant summer was near; Luke adds ‘and all the trees’, perhaps for readers who did not live among figs. In verse 34 kraipalē is the dizziness that follows heavy drinking, joined to drunkenness and the worries of life, the thorns that choke the word in the parable of the sower (8:14). A snare was a bird trap that sprang shut without warning, and Isaiah 24:17 pictures terror, pit, and snare for the dweller of the earth. At Passover the city overflowed with pilgrims, and many camped on the surrounding hills; Jesus spent his nights on the Mount of Olives (verse 37), at a place Judas knew (22:39).
literary:
The chapter opens with a brief scene (verses 1-4) that belongs with the warning about the scribes before it, and then gives the longest block of teaching in Luke's account of Jesus' last days. It is often called the Olivet discourse from its setting in Matthew and Mark, though Luke sets it in the temple. It answers the question of verse 7, when will these things happen and what will be the sign, and Luke arranges the answer with time markers. Deceivers and wars come first, ‘but the end is not imminent’ (verse 9). ‘Before all this’ comes persecution of the disciples (verse 12). Then the siege, with ‘when you see Jerusalem surrounded by armies’ (verse 20), and captivity ‘until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled’ (verse 24). Then signs in the heavens and the coming of the Son of Man (verses 25-28). A parable (29-33) and a closing exhortation (34-36) follow, and a narrative summary (37-38) closes the temple section.

Comparing Mark 13 shows Luke's hand. He adds that false teachers will say ‘The time is near’ and tells the disciples not to follow them (verse 8), and he says the end will not come ‘immediately’ (verse 9), which fits his correction of imminent expectation at 19:11. He omits Mark's ‘beginning of birth pains’, the shortening of the days for the elect, and the saying that no one knows the day or hour, not even the Son (Mark 13:32), though Acts 1:7 makes a similar point. Where Mark has the Holy Spirit give the disciples words (Mark 13:11), Luke has Jesus promise, ‘I will give you speech and wisdom’, literally ‘a mouth and wisdom’ (verse 15), which Acts shows fulfilled when Stephen's opponents could not stand up to his wisdom (Acts 6:10). Most strikingly, Luke replaces Mark's cryptic ‘abomination of desolation’ with the plain ‘Jerusalem surrounded by armies’ (verse 20). Some see here knowledge of the Roman siege; others, following C. H. Dodd (1947), see a translation of Daniel's riddle into the Old Testament language of sieges for Gentile readers. Hans Conzelmann (Die Mitte der Zeit, 1954, translated as The Theology of St Luke, 1960) argued that Luke thus separated the fall of Jerusalem, a historical event, from the end, to explain the delay of Christ's return; I. Howard Marshall (Luke: Historian and Theologian, 1970) and others replied that Luke keeps the note of nearness (verses 28, 31, 36) alongside the delay.

The closing exhortation (verses 34-36) is found only in Luke and shares vocabulary with Paul's teaching in 1 Thessalonians 5:1-8: ‘suddenly’ (aiphnidios, found only in these two places in the New Testament), no escape, drunkenness, and the call to stay awake. The chapter's own pairings carry its message: the widow's gift against the temple's gifts, stones admired against stones thrown down, hearts weighed down against heads lifted up, and a temporary trampling against a word that will never pass away.

outline.t: The temple's destruction foretold; signs that are not yet the end
The coming of the Son of Man
The parable of the fig tree
Keep watch and pray; days in the temple, nights on the Mount

doctrines.note: The Son of Man will come “in a cloud with power and great glory” (verse 27), and his coming is the disciples' redemption drawing near (verse 28). Christians differ on how much of the discourse was fulfilled in AD 70, but the church's creeds confess from this and related texts that Christ will come again, and Luke's picture of his coming in a cloud matches the promise at his ascension (Acts 1:9-11).

Jesus announces that Herod's temple, the center of Israel's worship and one of the wonders of its age, will be thrown down stone by stone (verse 6). Luke will show God's presence among his people moving to the risen Christ and the Spirit poured out on the church (Acts 2), though the apostles keep praying in the temple while it stands (Acts 3:1).

Jesus promises his disciples persecution, betrayal by family, and even death, and in the same breath says that not a hair of their head will perish and that by patient endurance they will gain their souls (verses 16-19). The promise is not immunity from suffering but final safety in God's hands, held through endurance.

Jesus grieves over wrath upon ‘this people’ (verse 23), speaking as a Jewish prophet over his own city, as Jeremiah did. The trampling of Jerusalem lasts ‘until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled’ (verse 24), a limit that many readers connect with Luke's hope for Israel's restoration (Acts 1:6, 3:19-21) and with Paul's in Romans 11:25-26. How to read that limit is contested; see the hard questions.

Jesus measures the widow's gift not by its size but by what she had left: the rich gave out of their abundance, she out of her poverty (verse 4). God sees what others overlook, and the value of a gift lies in its cost to the giver. The story does not teach that the poor should give away what they need to live.

words.note: Husterēma, lack, need, what is missing. It occurs nine times in the New Testament, once in the Gospels (verse 4) and otherwise in Paul, for the needs of the poor in Jerusalem that the Corinthians' abundance could supply (2 Corinthians 8:14, 9:12) and for what is lacking in Christ's afflictions (Colossians 1:24). The contrast in verse 4 is exact: the rich gave out of their perisseuma, their surplus, and the widow out of her husterēma, her lack.

Erēmōsis, desolation, laying waste. It occurs only three times in the New Testament, once in each version of this discourse (Matthew 24:15, Mark 13:14, and here, verse 20). In the Greek of Daniel 9:27 and 12:11 it is part of the phrase ‘abomination of desolation’, and in 2 Chronicles 36:21 it names the desolation of the land after Babylon's conquest. Luke keeps the word but drops the abomination, speaking of the city's desolation by armies.

Pateō, to tread, trample. It occurs five times in the New Testament: treading on snakes and scorpions (10:19), Jerusalem trodden down by the Gentiles (verse 24), and three times in Revelation, where the nations trample the holy city for forty-two months (Revelation 11:2) and the winepress of God's wrath is trodden (14:20, 19:15). The image comes from the Greek of Zechariah 12:3 and Daniel 8:13, where the holy place is trampled for a set time.

Kairos, time, especially a fitting or appointed time. It occurs about 85 times in the New Testament and 13 in Luke. The chapter uses it three times with different weight: deceivers will say ‘the time is near’ (verse 8), Jerusalem is trodden down until the ‘times of the Gentiles’ are fulfilled (verse 24), and disciples are to keep watch ‘at all times’ (verse 36). At 19:44 Jerusalem failed to recognize the time of its visitation. Luke's teaching on time is less about calendars than about recognizing God's moments.

Hupomonē, endurance, steadfastness under pressure, literally remaining under a load. It occurs about 32 times in the New Testament, only twice in the Gospels, both in Luke: the good soil that bears fruit with perseverance (8:15) and here (verse 19). It is not passive waiting but active faithfulness under trial, and it becomes a favorite word of Paul, James, and Revelation for the church's life between Christ's comings (Romans 5:3-4, James 1:3-4, Revelation 1:9).

Apolutrōsis, redemption, the release of a captive or slave, originally by payment. It occurs ten times in the New Testament, only here in the Gospels (verse 28). Paul uses it both for the redemption believers already have in Christ (Romans 3:24, Ephesians 1:7) and for the redemption of the body still awaited (Romans 8:23). Luke's first chapters spoke of those waiting for the redemption of Jerusalem (2:38, with a related word), and the Emmaus disciples had hoped Jesus would redeem Israel (24:21).

Genea, generation, the people living at one time, and more broadly a family, race, or kind of people. It occurs about 43 times in the New Testament and 15 in Luke, usually of Jesus' contemporaries, often with rebuke (7:31, 9:41, 11:29-32, 11:50-51, 17:25). BDAG distinguishes descendants of a common ancestor, a group sharing characteristics, those living at the same time, and an age or period. How to read it in verse 32 is the chapter's central difficulty, discussed below.

Agrupneō, to stay awake, be alert, literally to go without sleep. It occurs four times in the New Testament: in Mark's and Luke's discourses (Mark 13:33, verse 36), in Paul's call to keep alert with perseverance in prayer (Ephesians 6:18), and of leaders who keep watch over souls (Hebrews 13:17). In Luke it is joined to prayer for strength, and within days the disciples will sleep while Jesus prays on the Mount of Olives (22:45-46).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as the prophet of Jerusalem's fall, in the line of Micah and Jeremiah, who foretold the destruction of the first temple (Micah 3:12, Jeremiah 7:12-14), and his word came true within forty years. But he claims more than a prophet could. He promises to give his persecuted disciples a mouth and wisdom (verse 15), as God promised to help Moses speak and teach him what to say (Exodus 4:12). He says that heaven and earth will pass away but his words will never pass away (verse 33), which Isaiah said of the word of God: “the word of our God stands forever” (Isaiah 40:8). And he presents himself as the Son of Man of Daniel 7:13, who will come in a cloud with power and great glory, before whom all people must finally stand (verse 36).

Luke's picture of that coming ties the end of his Gospel to the beginning of Acts. The Son of Man comes ‘in a cloud’ (singular, where Mark has clouds), and forty days after the resurrection a cloud takes Jesus from the apostles' sight, and angels promise that he will come back in the same way (Acts 1:9-11). His coming is not only a threat but the disciples' redemption drawing near (verse 28), the redemption of Jerusalem that Anna and Simeon awaited in the same temple courts (2:25, 2:38).

The discourse is also a map of his own passion. He will be seized and handed over, brought before a king and a governor (Herod and Pilate, 23:1-12), betrayed by one of his friends, and put to death. On the road to the cross he will repeat the warning about mothers and children in Jerusalem's coming days (23:28-29). He commands his disciples to watch and pray for strength to stand, and he himself prays on the Mount of Olives while they sleep (22:39-46). And his notice of the widow, whom no one else noticed, shows the character of the coming judge: he sees the smallest gift, and he himself is about to give all he has.
interpretation:
The church read this chapter from early on as history fulfilled and hope still to come. Eusebius of Caesarea, in the early fourth century, set Josephus's account of the siege beside Luke 21:20-24 and quoted the verses to show that Jesus' words had come true (Ecclesiastical History 3.5-7), and he framed the city's fall as God's judgment on the Jews for their crimes against Christ, a framing that shaped Christian attitudes for centuries. Augustine, in his long letter to Hesychius of Salona (Letter 199, around 419), argued that Luke's version showed that the abomination of Mark and Matthew referred to the siege of Jerusalem, and that the end itself could not be calculated. That distinction between the fall of the city and the final coming, drawn from Luke, passed into medieval and Reformation exegesis. Jewish memory of the same events lives in the fast of Tisha B'Av, when Lamentations is read, and in the Talmud's stories of the war (b. Gittin 55b-56b).

In worship, verses 25 to 33 were the Gospel for the First Sunday of Advent in the Roman Missal of 1570 and for the Second Sunday in Advent in the Book of Common Prayer (1662) and the Lutheran churches, and Bach's lost Weimar cantata for that Sunday in 1716 (BWV 70a), whose title calls the hearer to watch and pray, took its theme from verse 36. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 25 to 36 on the First Sunday of Advent and verses 5 to 19 in November of Year C (Proper 28); the Roman lectionary reads verses 25-28 and 34-36 on the First Sunday of Advent and verses 5 to 19 on the Thirty-third Sunday in Ordinary Time. The widow's offering has been painted by James Tissot, among others, in his Life of Christ series (1886 to 1894, now in the Brooklyn Museum), and Nicolas Poussin's The Destruction and Sack of the Temple of Jerusalem (1625 to 1626), painted for Cardinal Francesco Barberini, is now in the Israel Museum.

Modern interpretation divided along lines already visible in the fathers. Hans Conzelmann (1954) made Luke's separation of Jerusalem's fall from the end the key to Luke's whole theology of salvation history. C. H. Dodd (Journal of Roman Studies, 1947) argued that 21:20-24 is composed from Old Testament siege language, and Lloyd Gaston (No Stone on Another, 1970) studied the significance of Jerusalem's fall across the Synoptic Gospels. Among readers of prophecy, J. Stuart Russell (The Parousia, 1878) argued that the discourse was fulfilled in AD 70. The Scofield Reference Bible (1909) defined the times of the Gentiles as the long period from Nebuchadnezzar's conquest of Judah to Christ's return in glory. In 1876 Charles Taze Russell, following the Adventist Nelson Barbour, calculated that the Gentile Times would end in 1914, counting 2,520 years from a date he gave as 606 BC; the Watch Tower Society later used 607 BC, and Jehovah's Witnesses still teach a form of the calculation. After Israel took the Old City of Jerusalem in June 1967, some dispensational writers asked whether the times of the Gentiles had ended. Darrell Bock (Luke, 1996) reads verse 32 of the generation that sees the final signs, and Robert Tannehill (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1985) and Jacob Jervell (1972) read the chapter within Luke's larger story of Israel. Addison Wright's argument that the widow's gift is a lament rather than a model (Catholic Biblical Quarterly, 1982) applies to Luke with special force, since Luke sets it immediately after the scribes who defraud widows.
text:
English Bibles differ at a few points in this chapter. In verse 4 the King James Version reads ‘cast in unto the offerings of God’, following later manuscripts that add ‘of God’; the earliest have only ‘into the gifts’. In verse 19 the manuscripts divide over one letter. Codex Alexandrinus, Codex Vaticanus, and others read ktēsesthe, ‘you will gain your souls’, a promise, which the BSB and several English versions follow; Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Bezae, and the majority of later manuscripts read ktēsasthe, ‘gain your souls’, a command, which NA28 prints as the harder reading. Both fit the context: endurance is both commanded and rewarded.

The verse division between 34 and 35 differs. Greek editions place the words ‘like a snare’ (hōs pagis) at the start of verse 35, and the King James Version, following the Textus Receptus, reads ‘For as a snare shall it come on all them that dwell on the face of the whole earth’. The critical text's word order attaches the snare to the suddenness of that day, and the BSB, with the ESV and NIV, ends verse 34 with it. The meaning is close either way. In verse 36 the King James Version reads ‘that ye may be accounted worthy to escape’ (kataxiōthēte, the Textus Receptus and Byzantine reading), where the earliest manuscripts read katischusēte, ‘that you may have strength’ to escape.

Finally, a group of medieval manuscripts known as family 13 place the story of the woman caught in adultery, usually printed as John 7:53-8:11, after Luke 21:38, a setting that suits verses 37 and 38, where Jesus teaches in the temple by day and spends the night on the Mount of Olives (compare John 8:1-2). The story is absent from the earliest manuscripts of both Gospels, and its wandering placement is part of the evidence that it circulated independently.

teach.big: What looks permanent will fall and what looks small is seen by God, so Jesus' followers live between Jerusalem's fall and his coming by giving wholeheartedly, refusing deception, enduring persecution, and watching in prayer for the Son of Man.

outline.t: God measures a gift by what it costs, and he sees the poor whom the powerful overlook; the widow's devotion also indicts the leaders who should have protected her.
The most magnificent religious building of its age would be thrown down; what we admire most is not what lasts.
The first danger is deception, especially by those who say the time is near; wars and disasters are real but are not a timetable.
Before the end, disciples will be handed over as Jesus was, and persecution becomes witness; Jesus gives words, guards his own, and calls for endurance.
Jerusalem's fall is God's judgment within history, grieved by Jesus and bounded by the times of the Gentiles; when judgment comes, faith flees rather than clings to the old center.
History ends not in chaos but in the Son of Man; when the world faints with fear, his people lift up their heads because redemption is near.
The signs are as readable as a fig tree in spring, and Jesus' words outlast the universe.
The greatest danger is not persecution but a heart dulled by excess and worry; watch and pray for strength to stand before the Son of Man.
Jesus spends his last days doing what he calls his disciples to do: teaching by day, praying by night, and keeping faith under the shadow of the cross.

teach.pitfalls:
The commonest misuse of this chapter is to treat it as a code for dating the end, matching each war, earthquake, or political event to a verse. Luke's version warns against exactly this: those who say ‘The time is near’ are deceivers (verse 8), and the end does not follow immediately (verse 9). The long record of failed dates, including the calculations built on ‘the times of the Gentiles’, should make teachers humble. The opposite error explains away the Lord's return because verses 20 to 24 refer to AD 70; Luke himself sets the coming of the Son of Man after that event.

A second pitfall is to present one reading of the chapter as the only faithful one. Preterist, futurist, and mixed readings are held by careful interpreters who share the church's confession, and a teacher should say so. A third is to read verses 20 to 24 as God's verdict against the Jewish people, as Christian preaching long did. Jesus speaks as a Jew grieving over his city, the apostles in Acts keep worshiping in its temple, and Luke's story holds out hope for Israel. A fourth is to preach the widow's offering as a fundraising text that urges the poor to give beyond their means; Luke sets it directly after Jesus condemns leaders who defraud widows, and the story honors her devotion while it indicts those who should have cared for her.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on two kinds of fear. Some listeners have been frightened by end-times preaching, often as children, and carry anxiety about missing the signs or being left behind; Jesus' purpose in telling them beforehand was to steady them (verse 9, ‘do not be alarmed’) and to lift their heads (verse 28). Others know the persecution and family betrayal of verses 12 to 17 from experience, as converts rejected by their families or believers who have lost work or safety for their faith; the promises of words given (verse 15) and of final safety (verse 18) are for them. Be careful with verse 16 in a room where some have been betrayed by family for other reasons; it names the pain without making it a virtue. Verse 34 will touch those struggling with drinking or with crushing anxiety; Jesus names both as burdens that dull the heart, not as proof that someone is lost, and the call to pray for strength is also an invitation to seek help. The widow's story will speak to people who give sacrificially out of little and feel unseen. They are seen.

hard.q: Jesus said this generation would not pass away until all these things happened. Was he mistaken about the time of his return?
hard.a:
The objection is old and serious. Verse 32 is introduced with the solemn ‘Truly I tell you’, and in Luke genea usually means Jesus' contemporaries (7:31, 11:29-32). If ‘all these things’ includes the coming of the Son of Man in verse 27, then Jesus predicted that the end would come within his hearers' lifetimes, and it did not. Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906) built his portrait of Jesus as a prophet of the imminent end on sayings like this and concluded that history had proved him wrong; Bertrand Russell (Why I Am Not a Christian, 1927) cited the same expectation against Jesus' wisdom; and C. S. Lewis, a believer, called the parallel in Mark 13:30 the most embarrassing verse in the Bible (in the essay The World's Last Night). Jewish readers have added that the Messiah was to bring the age of peace the prophets foretold, and the world after Jesus did not see it.

Christian interpreters answer in three main ways, each with able defenders. The preterist reading, argued by J. Stuart Russell (The Parousia, 1878) and in moderate forms by R. T. France and N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996), takes ‘all these things’ as the events leading to the fall of Jerusalem, and in Wright's case reads the Son of Man's coming in Daniel 7's sense of vindication, all fulfilled within forty years. The futurist reading takes genea as the generation that sees the final signs; Darrell Bock (Luke, Baker Exegetical Commentary, 1996) argues that when the signs of the end begin, they will run their course within one generation, and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) proposed the Jewish people. The mixed reading notes that ‘these things’ in verse 28 and verse 31 are signs that come before the redemption and the kingdom, not the coming itself, so ‘all these things’ in verse 32 may mean the signs and the city's fall, while the coming follows at a time no one can calculate; Augustine argued along these lines (Letter 199). Luke's own arrangement supports some interval, since Jerusalem is trodden down ‘until the times of the Gentiles are fulfilled’ (verse 24) before the cosmic signs of verses 25 to 27, and Acts 1:7 says the times and seasons are the Father's. Each view carries a burden: the critical view must explain why Luke kept a saying he believed had failed, the futurist must answer Luke's usual sense of genea, and the preterist and mixed views must explain how closely verse 32 follows verse 27. The timing of Christ's return is a question on which faithful Christians differ; that he will come is confessed by all.

hard.q: What are ‘the times of the Gentiles’, and does verse 24 teach that God punished the Jewish people?
hard.a:
The strongest objection comes from the history of the verse's use. Eusebius (Ecclesiastical History 3.5-7) presented Jerusalem's fall, with these verses quoted beside Josephus, as God's punishment of the Jews for their crimes against Christ, and that reading ran through Christian preaching for centuries, including the Lutheran observance of the Tenth Sunday after Trinity at which Josephus's account of the siege was read. Jewish readers have rightly pointed out that this made Jesus' lament into a charter for contempt, and that Christians who quoted ‘wrath against this people’ (verse 23) rarely wept as Jesus did. A different objection comes from skeptics, who note that attempts to calculate ‘the times of the Gentiles’ have repeatedly failed: Charles Taze Russell's reckoning that they would end in 1914, and later claims tied to 1948 or 1967, set dates that passed without the end.

The responses start with what the verse says. ‘Days of vengeance, to fulfill all that is written’ (verse 22) is the language of the covenant curses and the prophets (Deuteronomy 28:64, 32:35; Hosea 9:7), spoken by a Jewish prophet over his own city, as Jeremiah spoke over it in 587 BC; it is judgment within Israel's own story, not a verdict that God has abandoned his people. The sentence is bounded by ‘until’, which many interpreters read as a hint of an end to the trampling and of hope beyond it. Readers take the times of the Gentiles in several ways. Some, reading historically, take them as the period of Roman domination that ends with Jerusalem's fall or with the age of Gentile rule that follows it. Others take them as the age of the Gentile mission, when the gospel goes to the nations (24:47, Acts 1:8), and many compare Paul's hope that a partial hardening has come on Israel until the full number of the Gentiles has come in (Romans 11:25-26). Dispensational interpreters, following the Scofield Reference Bible (1909), take them as the long age of Gentile rule over Jerusalem from Nebuchadnezzar to Christ's return, after which Israel will be restored. Jacob Jervell (1972) and Robert Tannehill (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1985) argued that Luke-Acts holds out hope for Israel's restoration (Acts 1:6, 3:19-21) even as it tells a story of tragic rejection. Faithful Christians differ on the details and on the place of the modern state of Israel in them. What the text does not support is either contempt for the Jewish people or confident date-setting; it gives a limit to judgment known only to God.

observe: What contrast does Jesus draw between the rich and the widow in verses 3 and 4, and what words describe what each gave out of?
List the time markers in verses 8 to 28 (‘first’, ‘before all this’, ‘when you see’, ‘until’, ‘at that time’). In what order do the events come?
What three things does Jesus warn will weigh the heart down in verse 34, and what does he tell his disciples to pray for in verse 36?
interpret: Why do you think Luke places the widow's offering directly after the warning about scribes who defraud widows (20:47)?
Luke has ‘Jerusalem surrounded by armies’ where Mark has ‘the abomination of desolation’. What difference does that make to how a reader understands verses 20 to 24?
How can Jesus say both that some of his disciples will be put to death (verse 16) and that not a hair of their head will perish (verse 18)?
apply: The disciples admired stones that would soon be thrown down. What impressive things in your life or church might look different in the light of Jesus' words?
Which is more likely to dull your watchfulness, excess or the worries of life? What would it look like to pray for strength this week?
If Jesus measures gifts by what they cost, how should that shape the way you give, and the way your church treats those who give out of little?
